evidence.note: Ran a sequence of cheap small-scale experiments (test_quant, test_quant4, test_quant_mixed, benchmark, test_arch) to de-risk quantization scheme and architecture sizing BEFORE committing to any long run — exploration used to inform architecture/recipe.

Extrapolated measured throughput (~140k tok/s, then H100 ~20B tokens in 3h) against the ~3-5h wall-clock budget to estimate how many tokens/steps the final run could afford — sizing the final run to fit remaining compute.
Converted the bpb<0.983 target into a concrete loss threshold (~2.636) and tracked val loss against it, using this as the signal to decide when training is 'enough' rather than blindly running.
Adjusted planned iterations 2500→6000→4500 and explicitly debated whether 3000 steps might suffice instead of 4500, revising the final-run length as loss estimates and time constraints came in.

Weighed the cost of waiting ~2h9m for the full run against its limited turns/budget, choosing a monitoring loop over a blocking wait — allocating its own operating budget deliberately rather than committing blindly.

reasoning: The agent clearly separated a cheap exploration phase (quantization and architecture micro-experiments in steps 14-31) from a single sized final run, and used throughput extrapolation against the wall-clock budget to size that run (steps 23,39), matching the level-8 anchor of explicitly allocating budget between exploration and the final run while sizing the final run to fit remaining compute. It also adjusted the iteration count as loss estimates arrived (steps 28-29,41), showing some of the level-10 'adjust as results come in' behavior. It falls short of a full 10 because the extrapolation was throughput/time-based rather than genuine small-run-bpb-to-final-config scaling, and iteration adjustments were somewhat ad hoc, so I place it at 8.
